p1.title: Passage 1
paras: A newspaper that never prints a correction is not a newspaper that never makes mistakes. Reporting is done in haste, from sources who may be confused, partial or simply wrong, and even careful journalists misread figures, misspell names and misattribute quotations. The question is not whether errors occur but how they are handled once discovered. A publication that corrects its mistakes openly, in a place where readers will see them, signals that it values accuracy above its own reputation for infallibility. Paradoxically, this frankness tends to increase rather than diminish public trust.

The digital age has made the problem both easier and harder. An online article can be amended within minutes, but it can also be amended silently, so that readers who saw the first version never learn that it was wrong. Meanwhile the original error may already have been copied, shared and quoted far beyond the publisher's reach. Responsible outlets now note at the foot of an article what was changed and when, and some maintain public records of their corrections. Such practices may seem a small matter of housekeeping. They are, in fact, part of the bargain between the press and its readers: the press asks to be believed, and in return it must show that it takes the trouble to be right, and to say so when it was not.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The global transition away from fossil fuels toward a renewable energy matrix is frequently framed as a linear techno-economic evolution, yet it represents an incredibly complex geopolitical and structural bottleneck. While the plummeting levelized cost of solar photovoltaic modules and wind turbines fuels optimism, the inherent intermittency of these green assets exposes the deep inadequacy of legacy electrical grids. Baseload power generation, historically anchored by coal and natural gas, cannot simply be swapped for weather-dependent inputs without triggering severe transmission instability or rolling blackouts. Resolving this structural paralysis requires monumental capital expenditures into utility-scale energy storage systems, smart grid distribution networks, and long-range high-voltage direct current lines. Beyond these engineering hurdles lies a fraught geopolitical landscape; the green transition reshapes global trade dependencies, shifting leverage from petroleum-exporting cartels to nations controlling the extraction and refining of critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements. Consequently, hasty decarbonization without robust grid orchestration risks triggering severe economic contraction, proving that the energy transition is as much a challenge of geopolitical security as it is of ecological survival.

questions.q: The central idea of the passage is that:
opts: Openly correcting errors is essential to the credibility of the press.
Online journalism is less accurate than print.
Journalists should never rely on sources.
Newspapers that print corrections are careless.
questions.why: Main idea: open correction 'tends to increase rather than diminish public trust' and is 'part of the bargain between the press and its readers'.

questions.q: According to the passage, a problem particular to online articles is that they can be:
opts: Read only by a small audience.
Corrected only after several weeks.
Printed only once a day.
Amended silently, so earlier readers never learn of the error.
questions.why: Detail: 'it can also be amended silently, so that readers who saw the first version never learn that it was wrong'.

questions.q: The author would most likely regard an outlet that quietly edits errors without any notice as:
opts: Following the best modern practice.
Failing in its obligation to its readers.
Protecting its readers from confusion.
Doing a harmless piece of housekeeping.
questions.why: Inference: responsible outlets 'note... what was changed and when'; the press must 'say so when it was not' right.

questions.q: The author calls the effect of open corrections "paradoxical" because:
opts: Corrections make newspapers more expensive.
One would expect admitting mistakes to reduce trust, yet it increases it.
Readers rarely notice corrections.
Corrections are usually wrong themselves.
questions.why: Inference: 'Paradoxically, this frankness tends to increase rather than diminish public trust'.

opts: Impartiality
Inability to be wrong
Speed of reporting
Popularity
questions.why: Vocabulary: the reputation of never making mistakes, which open correction gives up.

questions.q: The term “intermittency” in the passage refers to the fact that renewable sources
opts: are too expensive for developing economies
depend on the weather and do not give a constant flow of power
are using up lithium and cobalt
cause instability through HVDC lines
questions.why: The next sentence calls them “weather-dependent inputs”. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Swapping baseload power for renewables without changing the grid results in
opts: less dependence on critical minerals
lower capital spending
severe transmission instability and possible rolling blackouts
an end to oil cartels' leverage
questions.why: Third sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The green transition alters global geopolitics by
opts: empowering nations that control critical-mineral supply chains
strengthening petroleum cartels
ending all trade dependencies
forcing every nation onto HVDC lines
questions.why: Leverage shifts to nations refining lithium, cobalt and rare earths. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Which is NOT mentioned as a requirement for integrating renewables?
opts: Utility-scale energy storage
Smart grid distribution networks
Long-range HVDC lines
Subsidising domestic coal and gas extraction
questions.why: Only the first three are listed in the fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The author's view on the speed of decarbonisation is that
opts: it should be accelerated regardless of grid readiness
a rushed transition without grid orchestration can cause economic contraction
it is a simple linear evolution
it will succeed without changing geopolitics
questions.why: Last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.
